title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Waking at first light, Levin tried to rouse his companions. Vassenka was face down with one stockinged leg sticking out, asleep so deeply that no nudging got a response. Oblonsky, half conscious, refused to get up at that hour. Even Laska, curled into the hay, came to her feet reluctantly, then stretched and straightened her hind legs one after the other. Levin pulled on his stockings and boots, took his gun, eased the creaking barn door open, and stepped out into the road. The coachmen were asleep in their carriages, the horses were dozing. Only one of them was still chewing oats, its nose down in the manger. Outside, everything was still gray.
"Up so early, my dear?" said the old woman who was their hostess, coming out of the hut and speaking to him with the warmth of an old friend.
"Going shooting, granny. Is this the way to the marsh?"

"Straight out the back, dear — past our threshing floor and the hemp patches. There's a little footpath." Stepping carefully on her sunburnt bare feet, the old woman led Levin out and moved the fence aside for him by the threshing floor.
"Straight on and you'll come to the marsh. Our boys took the cattle out there last night."

Laska ran eagerly ahead along the little path. Levin followed at a brisk, light pace, glancing constantly at the sky. He hoped to reach the marsh before the sun was up. But the sun was not waiting. The moon, which had been bright when he set out, was now only a curve of quicksilver. The pink wash of dawn that had been impossible to miss earlier now had to be hunted for to be seen at all. What had been only vague blurs in the distance were now sharp and distinct. They were sheaves of rye. The dew, invisible until the sun rose, soaked Levin's legs and his shirt above the belt as he passed through the tall, fragrant hemp patch, where the pollen had already dropped. In the clean stillness of the morning every small sound carried. A bee shot past his ear with the whine of a bullet. He looked carefully and saw a second, then a third. They were all flying out from the hives behind the hedge and disappearing across the hemp patch in the direction of the marsh. The path went straight to it. He could pick the marsh out by the mist over it — thicker in some places, thinner in others — so that the reeds and willow clumps stood up like islands in the haze. Along the edge of the marsh, between it and the road, peasant boys and men who had been minding the horses overnight lay asleep under their coats in the half-light. A short way off three horses stood hobbled. One of them rattled a chain. Laska walked beside her master, pressing a little ahead, looking around. Past the sleeping peasants and at the first stand of reeds, Levin checked his pistols and let the dog go. One of the horses, a sleek dark-brown three-year-old, caught sight of the dog, shied, swished its tail and snorted. The other horses were spooked too, and they splashed through the water on their hobbled legs, dragging their hoofs out of the deep mud with a squelching sound as they crashed out of the marsh. Laska stopped, gave the horses an ironic look and her master a questioning one. He patted her and whistled to signal that she could start.
Laska bounded happily and nervously through the bog as it gave way under her.

Pushing into the marsh, in among the familiar smells of roots, marsh plants, and slime, with the foreign smell of horse dung mixed in, Laska picked up at once the scent that ran through the whole marsh — the strong scent of that bird that always excited her more than any other. Here and there, among the moss and the marsh growth, the scent was very strong, but it was impossible to tell from any one spot in which direction it grew stronger or weaker. To work out the direction she had to get farther downwind. Without feeling her legs under her, Laska sprang forward in stiff bounds — bounds short enough that she could stop dead at any of them — moving to the right, against the wind blowing in from the east before sunrise, and turned to face it. Sniffing the air with her nostrils wide, she knew right away that not only the tracks but the birds themselves were just ahead of her, and more than one. Laska slowed. They were here, but where exactly she still could not say. To pin down the spot she began circling, and just then her master's voice pulled her off. "Laska! here?" he called, pointing her toward a different direction. She stopped and asked him whether she might not be better off going on the way she had begun. But he repeated his command sharply, pointing to a patch of standing water where there could not possibly be anything. She did as he said, pretending to search to keep him happy, went around it, came back to her old position, and at once had the scent again. Now that he was no longer interfering she knew what to do, and without watching her feet — to her annoyance she stumbled over a tall stump into the water but righted herself with her strong, supple legs — she began the circle that would make everything clear to her. The scent grew on her, stronger and stronger, more and more defined, and all at once she knew with absolute certainty that one of them was right there, behind this tuft of reeds, five paces in front of her. She stopped, and her whole body went still and rigid. On her short legs she could not see anything ahead, but by the scent she knew it was sitting no more than five paces away. She stood, more and more aware of it, savoring it in anticipation. Her tail was stretched out tense and straight, only the tip of it twitching. Her mouth was slightly open, her ears up. One ear had folded back the wrong way as she ran in, and she was breathing hard but carefully, watching, still more carefully — more with her eyes than by turning her head — for her master. He was coming with the face she knew so well, though the eyes were always frightening to her. He stumbled over the stump as he came, and to her mind he was moving extraordinarily slowly. She thought he was crawling, but he was running.

Catching the way Laska had crouched, almost flattening to the ground, scraping deep prints with her hind paws, her mouth slightly open, Levin knew she was pointing at grouse, and with a silent prayer for luck — especially on the first bird — he ran up to her. When he came right up to her, he could, from his height, see beyond her, and he saw with his eyes what she was reading with her nose. In a gap between two little thickets, only a couple of yards away, he could see a grouse. It had turned its head and was listening. Then, with a quick preen and a folding of its wings, it slipped around a corner with an awkward flick of its tail.
"Fetch it, fetch it!" Levin shouted, giving Laska a shove from behind.

"But I can't go," Laska was thinking. "Where am I to go? From here I can feel them, but if I move forward I won't know where they are or who they are." But then he gave her a push with his knee and said in an excited whisper, "Fetch it, Laska."

"Well, if that's what he wants, I'll do it, but I can't answer for what happens now," she thought, and she shot forward as fast as her legs could carry her through the thick bushes. She had lost the scent now; she could only see and hear, and she understood nothing.

Ten paces from where she had been, a grouse rose with a guttural cry and the peculiar round whir of its wings. The instant the shot came, it dropped heavily, its white breast hitting the wet mire. A second bird did not wait — it broke behind Levin without the dog. By the time he turned, it was already some way off. But his shot caught it. After flying twenty paces farther, that second grouse pitched upward, spun in the air like a ball, and dropped heavily on a patch of dry ground.
"Now this is going to be something!" thought Levin, packing the warm, plump grouse into his game bag. "Eh, Laska — is it going to be a good day?"

When Levin had reloaded and moved on, the sun was fully up, though hidden behind storm clouds. The moon had lost all its sheen and hung in the sky like a white cloud. Not a single star was left. The sedge, which had been silver with dew, now shone like gold. The standing pools all looked like amber. The blue cast of the grass had turned to a yellow-green. Marsh birds twittered and swarmed around the brook and on the bushes, which sparkled with dew and threw long shadows. A hawk woke, settled on a haycock, turned its head this way and that, and looked at the marsh as if it disapproved. Crows wheeled across the field, and a barefoot boy was driving the horses to an old man who had risen from under his long coat and was combing his hair. The smoke from the gun lay over the green grass as white as milk.
One of the boys ran up to Levin.
"Uncle, there were ducks here yesterday!" he called, and walked along a little way behind him.
And it gave Levin double pleasure, in front of this boy who was so impressed, to bring down three snipe in a row.
